Artist Casey Curran creates kinetic sculptures that combine mechanical systems with forms inspired by plants and natural structures. In this prototype, layers of delicate petals are connected so that a single mechanical action produces a rippling movement across the entire structure. Instead of every element moving independently, the motion travels through the sculpture like a wave. This type of movement is central to Curran’s practice. Using motors, wires, cranks and carefully engineered mechanisms, he creates artificial flowers and organisms that bloom, flutter and contract.  The machinery is artificial, but the movement feels strangely organic ,engineering becomes a way of imitating the rhythms of living systems. #art #artist #fashion #avantgarde #design

Imagine opening your old Nintendo DS to play Pokémon and realizing that Bulbasaur is actually climbing OUT of the game. 🌱🎮 That was the idea behind this satisfying Pokémon sand art ASMR project, and I think it might be one of my favorite combinations of Pokémon nostalgia and handmade artwork. I wanted to create something that felt like a childhood video game suddenly becoming real. Instead of drawing Bulbasaur standing next to a handheld console, I recreated the Pokémon actually emerging from it. The blue Nintendo DS-style system forms the bottom of the artwork, while Bulbasaur climbs over the screen with grass and vines growing around the console. Almost like the Pokémon world is slowly spreading into ours. And honestly, isn't that what we all wished would happen when we were kids? I remember how magical it felt to carry an entire Pokémon adventure around on a little handheld gaming system. You could explore different regions, catch Pokémon, build your team, and spend hours wandering through tall grass looking for something rare. But no matter how much time you spent playing, the Pokémon always stayed inside the screen. This artwork imagines what it might look like if one of them finally found a way out. Bulbasaur was such a fun choice because the plant growing on its back fits perfectly with the concept. Instead of just having the character appear from the console, the leaves and tall grass make it look like the handheld system is becoming overgrown with the Pokémon's natural environment. The little Poké Ball on the bottom screen helps complete the gaming connection, while the blue console, directional pad, and familiar buttons immediately give it that Nintendo DS nostalgia. And the entire design is recreated using colored sand! Every area is carefully filled with fine grains of sand, from Bulbasaur's turquoise-green body and bright red eyes to the large green leaves, blue handheld console, black outlines, and smaller screen details. The satisfying sand art ASMR process is especially interesting with designs like this because there are two very different types of artwork coming together. Bulbasaur has rounded organic shapes, facial expressions, and plant details. The handheld console is much more geometric, with straight edges, rectangular screens, and small circular buttons. Watching those different sections gradually connect is one of my favorite parts of creating sand art. At first you're seeing separate patches of blue, green, cream, red, and black. But as the details are completed, they begin forming a scene that looks like a Pokémon literally escaping from a video game. This project combines Bulbasaur fan art, Pokémon nostalgia, Nintendo DS-inspired artwork, retro gaming, satisfying colored sand painting, relaxing ASMR, handheld gaming memories, and creative Pokémon illustrations. It's also a fun reminder of how much Pokémon has been part of so many people's childhoods. Some people remember their first Game Boy. Others remember playing Pokémon Diamond, Pearl, Platinum, HeartGold, or SoulSilver on the Nintendo DS. But I think we all had the same thought at least once: What if Pokémon were real?
